::: {.solutions}

**12 questions.** Suggested time: **60 minutes**, no calculator.

Every question comes from a TMUA past paper, a TMUA mock or the official Notes on Logic and Proof, and its source
is shown beside the question number. None of them appears in the S1 or S2 class questions.

For every question the routine is the same: **name the halves $P$ and $Q$, write the statement as one arrow, then
classify** — reverse only is the *converse*, negate only is the *inverse*, and negate *and* reverse is the
*contrapositive*.

| Section | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **A — The relatives of a statement** | the three relatives, breaking a statement, and negating it | 1–4 |
| **B — What follows, and what does not** | holding a hypothesis and testing each claimed conclusion | 5–10 |
| **C — Proving the right direction** | noticing when a student has proved the converse | 11–12 |

# Section A — The relatives of a statement

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise K, Q2–3</span>

::: {.question}
Let $S$ be the statement "if $A$ then $B$".

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** What is the contrapositive of the converse of $S$? Is it logically equivalent to $S$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** What is the converse of the contrapositive of $S$? Is it logically equivalent to $S$?

::: {.question}

$$u_1=15,\quad u_2=21,\quad u_3=30,\quad u_4=37,\quad u_5=44,\quad u_6=51,\quad u_7=59$$

Consider the following statement about this sequence:

> $(*)$ If $n$ is a prime number, then $u_n$ is a multiple of $3$ or $u_n$ is a multiple of $5$.

What is the smallest value of $n$ that provides a counterexample to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $6$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $7$

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n$ denote a positive integer. Consider the following three statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** For every $n$, if $n^2$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** For every $n$, if $n^2$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** There exists an $n$ such that $n^2$ is divisible by $12$ but $n$ is not divisible by $12$.

Which of the statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** all of them
:::

::: {.question}
Consider the statement about Fred:

> $(*)$ Every day next week, Fred will do at least one maths problem.

If statement $(*)$ is **not** true, which of the following is certainly true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Every day next week, Fred will do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Some day next week, Fred will do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** On no day next week will Fred do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Every day next week, Fred will do no maths problems.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Some day next week, Fred will do no maths problems.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** On no day next week will Fred do no maths problems.

# Section C — Proving the right direction

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to solve the following problem, where $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers:

> Show that if $a^2-4b^3\ge0$ then there exist real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$.

Consider the following attempt:

&nbsp;&nbsp;$(x-y)^2\ge0$ &nbsp; **(I)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $x^2+y^2-2xy\ge0$ &nbsp; **(II)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $(x+y)^2-4xy\ge0$ &nbsp; **(III)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $x^2y^2(x+y)^2-4x^3y^3\ge0$ &nbsp; **(IV)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $a^2-4b^3\ge0$ &nbsp; **(V)**

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, but it would be correct if written in the reverse order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, but the student has correctly proved the converse.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (IV).
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A student answered the following question:

> $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers.
>
> Prove that the equation $x^3+ax^2+b=0$ has three distinct real roots if $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$

Here is the student's solution:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** We differentiate $y=x^3+ax^2+b$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+2ax=x(3x+2a)$. Solving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ shows that the stationary points are at $(0,b)$ and $\left(-\dfrac{2a}{3},\ b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** If $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$, then $b$ and $b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}$ must have opposite signs, and so one of the stationary points is above the $x$-axis and one is below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** If the cubic has three distinct real roots, then one of the stationary points is above the $x$-axis and one is below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** Hence if $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$, then the equation has three distinct real roots.

Which one of the following options best describes the student's solution?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is a completely correct solution.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The student has instead proved the converse of the statement in the question.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The solution is wrong, because the student should have stated step II after step III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step III.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:10cm"}
Working
:::
